text: matplotlib gives you complete control, but you write a lot of code for common statistical charts. seaborn is built on top of it, reads pandas DataFrames directly, computes summaries for you, and ships with attractive defaults. It's the fastest route from a DataFrame to an insight.

seaborn draws onto matplotlib axes, so figures, titles, and savefig from earlier lessons still apply. Every function takes the DataFrame with data equals, then names the columns for x, y, and hue. Hue splits the chart by a category, colors each group, and builds the legend for you.

Three panels, three one-line calls. histplot shows spend's distribution split by segment; Premium sits further right. boxplot compares the spread by segment: median spend is about two twenty-three for Basic, two ninety-three for Plus, three eighty-two for Premium. scatterplot shows orders against spend, colored by segment, with the upward trend holding inside every group.

Raw matplotlib would take many more lines to get there: grouping, looping over segments, choosing colors, building the legend by hand. seaborn's functions come in families: distributions, categorical comparisons, relationships, and matrices or overviews like heatmap and pairplot.

barplot calculates the mean of each group with an uncertainty interval, so you can hand it raw rows instead of pre-grouped data. lmplot, which you saw back in lesson one on Anscombe's quartet, adds a fitted line automatically.

A correlation heatmap with annot equals True writes each number in its cell, and the diverging coolwarm palette centered on zero follows lesson three's rule. Orders and spend correlate at point six seven; age relates to neither. pairplot draws a scatter for every pair of numeric columns at once, a fast first look at a new table.

Use histplot, boxplot and scatterplot for the basics, heatmap and pairplot for overviews, and remember every one of these still draws on ordinary matplotlib axes. Next lesson: Plotly, for charts you can hover, zoom and share.
